reading.body:
AI litigation is argued out of precedents decided long before generative models existed, not out of new law written for them.

The cases that matter are copyright, scraping and defamation, and the defenses rest on a small set of older decisions. Sony supplies substantial non-infringing use. Campbell and Google Books supply transformative purpose. Van Buren and hiQ supply scraping. Zeran supplies Section 230. Each of these was decided on facts that had nothing to do with training runs or model outputs, and each is now being stretched to cover them.

For AI specifically, this means the legal risk around training data and model behavior is being resolved by analogy rather than by statute. A defendant's exposure turns on how a judge maps a model onto a doctrine built for a VCR, a song parody, a web scraper or a message board. That mapping is contested, and it is happening case by case.

The data here covers United States courts only, and it does not say which way any case has gone or how many are pending. It names the precedents in play and the subject areas, not outcomes, damages or timing. Nothing in it speaks to compute, buildings or power, so no claim about the grid can be drawn from it.
